settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: SpEL is evaluated with the domain object as root (PatchOperation.getValue/setValue on `target`); this is not a full EvaluationContext with `T(...)` static-type access necessarily enabled, and I did not read any configuration that enables TypeLocator static access, so `T(...)` may not resolve.

Non-numeric segments appended (e.g. `foo.bars[1].baz` from `/foo/bars/1/baz`) are the intended design for property navigation, so not every raw append is anomalous; the security question is only about characters that change expression structure.
No test or configuration in the inspected ranges demonstrates an actual injection succeeding.
candidates.description: PathToSpEL.pathNodesToSpEL builds a SpEL expression string directly from the client-controlled JSON Patch path segments. Any non-numeric segment (pathNode) is appended verbatim (line 102), and the resulting string is parsed by a SpelExpressionParser in pathToExpression (line 43) / spelToExpression (line 53). There is no allow-list or escaping of characters such as `'`, `(`, `)`, `T(...)`, `#`, or `@` that are meaningful in SpEL. The `path` value originates from the JSON Patch document (`opNode.get("path").textValue()` in JsonPatchPatchConverter line 64) which is read straight from the request body (JsonPatchHandler.getPatchOperations line 112). Path segments that are not parseable as integers are the ones injected into the expression, so if a domain's JSON Patch allows arbitrary segment text, crafted values could influence the parsed expression. This is a candidate root cause (expression injection into SpEL via patch path); whether it is exploitable depends on the evaluation context/root object and reachable types, which I could not confirm statically.
missing_evidence: No inspection of how the SpEL root/EvaluationContext is configured at the point of getValue/setValue (Spring's Expression.getValue(Object) uses a SimpleEvaluationContext-free StandardEvaluationContext), which determines whether method invocation or static access is reachable.
No tracing of whether an authorization/access-control layer (e.g., Spring Security) restricts which properties a patch may touch.
No examination of tests for the patch package that might document intended path constraints/escaping.
preconditions: The application exposes the Spring Data REST JSON Patch (application/json-patch+json) PATCH endpoint for an exported repository/entity (default RepositoryEntityController.patchItemResource mapping BASE_MAPPING + '/{id}').
The attacker can supply an explicit path string that is not exclusively numeric segments (e.g., a segment containing SpEL-significant characters).
The resulting SpEL expression must be evaluated against a root object whose type/context permits the injected expression to do something the attacker wants.
candidates.title: Untrusted JSON Patch path converted to SpEL expression without escaping in PathToSpEL

counter_evidence: Patches are applied to a freshly read/existing domain object and then persisted by the repository invoker; normal property navigation is the documented feature.
Expression evaluation errors are wrapped as PatchException/HttpMessageNotReadableException, which limits blind probing in production responses (though not necessarily side effects).
The SpEL root is the domain object itself, not an arbitrary map/context, which constrains what expressions can reference.
candidates.description: PatchOperation stores a SpEL Expression derived from the request-provided path (PathToSpEL.pathToExpression at line 66) and subsequently evaluates it for both reads and writes: getValueFromTarget (line 177), popValueAtPath setValue (line 106), addValue setValue (lines 145/148), and setValueOnTarget (line 165). ReplaceOperation.perform (line 41) and TestOperation.perform (lines 53-54) call these. Because the expression is built from an untrusted string (see the PathToSpEL candidate), this assignment/evaluation against a live entity is the security-sensitive sink. This is reported as the sink half of the same expression-injection concern; it is a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability, because I could not verify the SpEL evaluation context restrictions or that the injected text can alter expression semantics rather than just fail.
missing_evidence: Whether the SpEL evaluation permits method invocation / bean references / type references in the runtime context used at getValue/setValue.
Whether property values reachable via the path are subject to any field-level or role-based access checks before assignment.
Behavior when a segment is not a valid property/index (error vs. silent no-op) which affects exploit reliability.
preconditions: A PATCH request with JSON Patch content type reaches JsonPatchHandler.apply on an existing target object.
The patch operation (replace/add/test/remove) references a path that PathToSpEL turns into the stored SpEL expression, which is then set/get on the target.
The target object graph exposes a writable property or index that the expression resolves to.
candidates.title: Patch operations evaluate/assign SpEL values on existing domain objects (setValue) driven by request path

counter_evidence: The converter returns the entity (or null) by id only; whether it represents an access-control decision depends on callers, which I did not fully inspect.
The comment/error message indicates the design intent is local-only resolution, suggesting callers are expected to supply local URIs.
convert is only invoked by Spring's conversion machinery when matches() returns true, requiring a repository for the target type.
candidates.description: UriToEntityConverter.convert takes a URI and splits its path on '/', requiring only that there be at least two parts (line 121), then uses only the LAST path segment as the id passed to invokeFindById (line 126). The error message for insufficient parts mentions 'Is it local or remote? Only local URIs are resolvable' but the code does not actually verify the URI host/scheme against any configured base URI or known mapping. This means an incoming URI referencing an arbitrary host but ending with a matching id path segment will be resolved to a local entity. This is a candidate for an unexpected/ambiguous reference-resolution behavior; impact depends on how URIs enter this converter and whether later authorization treats the resolved entity as trusted. I did not find confirmation of an exploitable authorization bypass, so it is reported as a candidate only.
missing_evidence: No enumeration of all call sites passing a URI into this converter (e.g., DomainObjectReader / Jackson deserialization of link fields).
No check of whether the host/scheme is validated earlier (e.g., by the framework's URI handling) before reaching convert.
No test demonstrating cross-host URI behavior in the inspected ranges.
preconditions: The converter is registered in the conversion service used by JSON deserialization of entity references (URI -> entity).
An attacker can supply a URI string (e.g., as a JSON property value) whose final '/' segment matches the id format of a target entity type.
Some downstream logic relies on the URI's origin (host/path) being authoritative for authorization or access decisions.
candidates.title: UriToEntityConverter resolves an entity from last URI path segment without validating it is a local/expected URI
